population|N: The entire group you actually want to know about (every unit, not just the ones you measured); its size is **N**. Numerical summaries of a population are called **parameters** (e.g. $\mu$, $\sigma$). See [What statistics is](#/math3042/what-is-statistics).
sample|n: A subset of the population that you actually collect data from; its size is **n**. Numerical summaries of a sample are called **statistics** (e.g. $\bar{X}$, $s$) and are used to estimate the population's parameters. $n-1$ (not $n$) is the divisor in the sample standard deviation $s$. See [What statistics is](#/math3042/what-is-statistics).
parameter|μ|\\mu|mu: A numerical summary of a **population** (e.g. the population mean $\mu = \dfrac{\sum X}{N}$) — usually unknown, and estimated from a sample statistic. See [Mean](#/math3042/mean).
statistic|X̄|\\bar{X}|\\bar{x}|X-bar|x̄|: A numerical summary of a **sample** — e.g. the **sample mean** $\bar{X} = \dfrac{\sum X}{n}$ for raw data or $\dfrac{\sum f_i X_i}{\sum f_i}$ for grouped data — used to estimate the corresponding population parameter. "Mean" without qualification usually means this arithmetic average; it is sensitive to outliers, unlike the median. See [Mean](#/math3042/mean).
s|standard deviation: The **sample standard deviation**: $s = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (X-\bar{X})^2}{n-1}}$ (divide by $n-1$, not $n$). "Standard deviation" in general is the typical distance of a data value from the mean — $s$ for a sample, $\sigma$ for a population (divide by $N$) — in the same units as the original data. See [Range & standard deviation](#/math3042/range-sd).
σ|\\sigma|sigma: The **population standard deviation**: $\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (X-\mu)^2}{N}}$ (divide by $N$). It's what the empirical rule and $Z$-scores are stated in terms of. See [Range & standard deviation](#/math3042/range-sd).
p̂|\\hat{p}|p-hat|categorical|proportion: The **sample proportion**: $\hat{p} = \dfrac{x}{n}$, the fraction of a sample falling in a category. **Categorical** data (a category/label like sex or colour, not a quantity) is summarized this way — with a proportion $\hat{p}$ per category and a mode — instead of a mean. See [Categorical data](#/math3042/categorical).
p: The **population proportion**: $p = \dfrac{X}{N}$, the true fraction of the population in a category, estimated by the sample proportion $\hat{p}$. See [Categorical data](#/math3042/categorical).
r|ρ|\\rho|rho|correlation|causation: **Correlation** is the strength and direction of a *linear* relationship between two numerical variables, measured by the sample correlation coefficient $r$ ($-1 \le r \le 1$): $r = \dfrac{n\sum xy - \sum x \sum y}{\sqrt{n\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2}\sqrt{n\sum y^2-(\sum y)^2}}$, or by the population parameter $\rho$. $r \approx 0$ means no linear relationship; $r$ near $\pm1$ is strong. Correlation never proves **causation** — two variables can be strongly correlated with no causal link, e.g. both driven by a confounding factor. See [Linear correlation r](#/math3042/correlation).
Q₁|Q_1|Q1: The **first quartile**: the value with about 25% of the (sorted) data at or below it, $Q_1 = P_{25}$. Forms the left edge of the box in a boxplot. See [Quartiles & percentiles](#/math3042/quartiles-percentiles).
Q₂|Q_2|Q2|median: The **second quartile**, equal to the **median**: $Q_2 = P_{50}$, the middle value of sorted data (average of the two middle values if $n$ is even). Unlike the mean, it is not pulled by outliers. See [Quartiles & percentiles](#/math3042/quartiles-percentiles).
Q₃|Q_3|Q3: The **third quartile**: the value with about 75% of the (sorted) data at or below it, $Q_3 = P_{75}$. Forms the right edge of the box in a boxplot. See [Quartiles & percentiles](#/math3042/quartiles-percentiles).
IQR|IQR(x)|whisker|outlier|fence: The **interquartile range**: $IQR = Q_3 - Q_1$, the width of the middle 50% of the data (in R, `IQR(x)`). It builds the **fences** that flag **outliers**: lower fence $= Q_1 - 1.5\times IQR$, upper fence $= Q_3 + 1.5\times IQR$. A boxplot's **whisker** extends only to the most extreme data value still inside the fences; anything beyond is drawn as an outlier point. See [IQR, boxplots & outliers](#/math3042/iqr-boxplot-outliers).
R|range: The **range**: $R = \text{maximum } X - \text{minimum } X$, the simplest (and crudest, since it uses only the two extreme points) measure of spread. See [Range & standard deviation](#/math3042/range-sd).
Sk|skewed left|skewed right: **Pearson's skewness coefficient**: $Sk = \dfrac{3(\bar{X}-Q_2)}{s}$ (sample) or $\dfrac{3(\mu-Q_2)}{\sigma}$ (population). $Sk = 0$ is symmetric, $Sk < 0$ is **skewed left** (longer tail toward small values, mean below median), $Sk > 0$ is **skewed right** (longer tail toward large values, mean above median); $|Sk| > 1$ is considered highly skewed. See [Skewness](#/math3042/skewness).
Z|unusual: A **Z-score**: $Z = \dfrac{X-\mu}{\sigma}$ (or $\dfrac{X-\bar{X}}{s}$ for sample data) — how many standard deviations $X$ is from the mean. $|Z| > 2$ is flagged **unusual** (outside the $\mu \pm 2\sigma$ band that holds about 95% of normal data), and $|Z| > 3$ is a likely outlier. See [Z-scores & unusual values](#/math3042/z-scores).
P_k|P_{k}|quartile|percentile|five-numbe: The **$k$th percentile**: the value with about $k\%$ of the sorted data at or below it. **Quartiles** are the 25th/50th/75th percentiles ($Q_1, Q_2, Q_3$); the **five-number summary** {minimum, $Q_1$, $Q_2$, $Q_3$, maximum} is what a boxplot draws. See [Quartiles & percentiles](#/math3042/quartiles-percentiles).
numerical: Data that records a measured or counted quantity (height, count of events) on which arithmetic is meaningful, so mean/median/sd all apply — unlike categorical data. See [What statistics is](#/math3042/what-is-statistics).
mode|mode(): The most frequently occurring value (numerical data) or category (categorical data); the only measure of centre that always applies to categorical data. R has no base function for it: `as.double(names(which.max(table(x))))`. See [Median & mode](#/math3042/median-mode).
grouped data|frequency|f_i: **Grouped data** is presented as class intervals with a **frequency** $f_i$ each, rather than individual raw values; $\sum f_i$ is the total sample size, and its mean/sd are computed by weighting each class's midpoint by $f_i$. See [Mean](#/math3042/mean).
class mark|X_i: The midpoint of a class interval in grouped data, used as the representative value $X_i$ for every observation in that class, paired with its frequency $f_i$ in $\bar{X} = \dfrac{\sum f_i X_i}{\sum f_i}$. See [Mean](#/math3042/mean).
variance|s^2|σ^2|\\sigma^2: Standard deviation squared ($s^2$ for a sample, $\sigma^2$ for a population): the mean squared deviation from the mean. Same information as $s$/$\sigma$ but in squared units, so it's rarely reported directly. See [Range & standard deviation](#/math3042/range-sd).
coefficient of variation|CV: A unit-free measure of relative spread: $CV = \dfrac{s}{\bar{X}} \times 100\%$ (sample) or $\dfrac{\sigma}{\mu}\times 100\%$ (population). Lets you compare variability between two data sets measured in different units or with different means. See [Coefficient of variation](#/math3042/cv).
normal distribution|empirical rule|\\mu: The **normal distribution** is the symmetric bell-shaped distribution defined by $\mu$ and $\sigma$. The **empirical rule**: for approximately normal data, about 68% falls within $\mu \pm 1\sigma$, about 95% within $\mu \pm 2\sigma$, and about 99.7% within $\mu \pm 3\sigma$. See [68–95–99.7 rule](#/math3042/empirical-rule).
Chebyshev|Chebyshev's rule|1 - \\frac{1}: A distribution-free bound that works for *any* data set, normal or not: at least $1 - \dfrac{1}{k^2}$ of the data lies within $\mu \pm k\sigma$ (e.g. $k=2$ guarantees at least 75%, versus the empirical rule's ~95% for normal data specifically). See [Chebyshev's rule](#/math3042/chebyshev).
boxplot|boxplot()|boxplot(x): A plot of the five-number summary: a box from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$ (split by a line at $Q_2$), whiskers out to the most extreme non-outlier values, and outliers drawn as individual points. In R: `boxplot(x)` for one vector, or `boxplot(y ~ group, data = df)` for one box per group. See [IQR, boxplots & outliers](#/math3042/iqr-boxplot-outliers).
mean()|mean(x): R function computing the arithmetic mean of a numeric vector, e.g. `mean(x)` or `mean(c(22, 19, 20, 22, 35, 19, 21, 23))`. See [R from Lab 1](#/math3042/r-essentials).
median()|median(x): R function computing the median of a numeric vector, e.g. `median(x)` or `median(faithful$eruptions[1:10])`. See [R from Lab 1](#/math3042/r-essentials).
sd()|sd(x)|sd: R function computing the **sample** standard deviation ($n-1$ denominator) of a numeric vector, e.g. `sd(x)` or `sd(c(5.0, 4.5, 6.0, 7.0, 5.2))`. See [R from Lab 1](#/math3042/r-essentials).
quantile()|quantile(x): R function returning percentiles/quartiles of a numeric vector; `quantile(x)` gives the default five-number-summary quartiles, `quantile(x, k/100)` gives the $k$th percentile. See [R from Lab 1](#/math3042/r-essentials).
hist()|hist(x, breaks = ..., right = FAL: R function drawing a histogram of a numeric vector; the `breaks` argument controls bin edges and `right = FALSE` makes bins left-closed (`[a, b)` instead of `(a, b]`). See [R from Lab 1](#/math3042/r-essentials).
cor()|cor(x, y): R function computing the sample correlation coefficient $r$ between two numeric vectors, e.g. `cor(x, y)`. See [R from Lab 1](#/math3042/r-essentials).
table(): R function producing a frequency (count) table of a categorical or discrete vector, e.g. `table(survey$Pulse)`; feeds into `which.max` to find the mode. See [R from Lab 1](#/math3042/r-essentials).
levels()|levels(TenMileRace$sex): R function listing the distinct categories (factor levels) of a categorical variable, e.g. `levels(TenMileRace$sex)`. See [R from Lab 1](#/math3042/r-essentials).
subset()|subset(df, condition): R function filtering a data frame's rows by a logical condition, e.g. `subset(df, condition)` — the base-R equivalent of `dplyr::filter()`. See [R from Lab 1](#/math3042/r-essentials).
filter()|dplyr::filter(): The `dplyr` package's row-filtering function, e.g. `dplyr::filter(df, condition)`; does the same job as base R's `subset()`. See [R from Lab 1](#/math3042/r-essentials).
droplevels(): R function that removes unused factor levels left over after subsetting a categorical variable, so tables/plots don't show empty categories. See [R from Lab 1](#/math3042/r-essentials).
which.max(): R function returning the index/name of the largest element of a vector; `as.double(names(which.max(table(x))))` is the standard idiom for finding the mode of numeric data. See [R from Lab 1](#/math3042/r-essentials).
rank(): R function converting a numeric vector into ranks (1 = smallest); `ties.method="min"` controls how tied values are ranked. See [R from Lab 1](#/math3042/r-essentials).
nrow(): R function returning the number of rows in a data frame or matrix, e.g. `nrow(df)` — often used as a quick sample-size check before computing statistics. See [R from Lab 1](#/math3042/r-essentials).
c(): R function that combines values into a vector, e.g. `c(22, 19, 20, 22, 35, 19, 21, 23)` — the basic way to build a data vector by hand. See [R from Lab 1](#/math3042/r-essentials).
$|object.field: R's operator for pulling a named column out of a data frame (or field out of a list), e.g. `faithful$eruptions` or `TenMileRace$net`. See [R from Lab 1](#/math3042/r-essentials).
